passages.question: What did the researcher build, and what can I establish with it?
passages.before: The completed Explorer contains 1,393 records. Its 943 \emph{Papers} are bibliographic entries for individual publications. The 247 \emph{Models} describe published models and link them to their source papers. The 157 \emph{Review Papers} records organize reviews and the publications they cover. The 42 \emph{Feedback pathways} name sensory connections reported in the literature. The 4 \emph{Recorders} identify people who entered pathway information in Airtable. A publication can appear in the bibliography and also have a linked model or review record. These numbers count entries of each kind.
passages.after: The SADb Explorer app lets researchers trace a proposed sensory connection back to its experimental source. The full curated collection is searchable in a browser, including records that no longer fit in the Airtable working base. The \emph{Table} view brings together the experimental conditions, the response, and its source. The \emph{Pivot} table groups papers by classifications such as afferent type and species. The \emph{Bubble map} connects a paper to the studies it cites and to later papers that cite it. A researcher can follow any of these comparisons back to an individual paper.
passages.judgment: The searchable app retains records beyond the working Airtable limit. Its Table, Pivot, and Bubble views each identify which individual study supports an observation.

passages.question: What observation puts this study under two apparently conflicting pathway names?
passages.before: Does input from one ankle extensor reinforce activity in another? A researcher can follow the McCrea example in the standalone website by opening \path{SADb_audit/app/sadb_app.html} from the project repository in a browser. In \emph{Table}, choosing \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} in the \emph{Pathway} filter retrieves six papers. Selecting the McCrea row opens its record (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_explorer}). The DOI leads to the original experiment. Two further fields answer different questions. \emph{Curation note} describes the response that the authors measured. \emph{Robot / sim translation} proposes a controller test based on that response.
passages.after: The study by \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} appears under both \emph{Ib disynaptic inhibition} and \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} in the app (Figure~\ref{fig:sadb_explorer}). Their Figure~3 shows why. The same plantaris nerve stimulus inhibited a medial gastrocnemius motor neuron at rest and excited it during extension in midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion.
passages.judgment: The same input to the same motor neuron had opposite effects at rest and during extension. The reader reaches a signed rule and can distinguish what the stimulus isolates from the circuit interpretation.

passages.question: What are the engineering parameters called, and what did the physical tests establish?
passages.before: The corrections identified on the pinned knee reduced torque-prediction error for both flexor and extensor configurations on the biomimetic knee. On the pinned flexor, replacing the force model of \citet{hunt_modeling_2017} improved the prediction, but the rigid-attachment calculation still overestimated measured torque magnitude. The hybrid calculation used measured muscle length and moment arm to separate force-model error from geometric error. In the final physical tests, both redesigned routes met or exceeded their selected human-muscle torque magnitudes at the measured knee angles (Section~\ref{sec:redesign_physical}).
passages.after: The design factors identified on the pinned knee reduced torque-prediction error for both flexor and extensor configurations on the biomimetic knee. On the pinned flexor, replacing the force model of \citet{hunt_modeling_2017} improved the prediction, but the rigid-attachment calculation still overestimated measured torque magnitude. The hybrid calculation used measured muscle length and moment arm to separate force-model error from geometric error. In the final physical tests, both redesigned routes met or exceeded their selected human-muscle torque magnitudes at the measured knee angles (Section~\ref{sec:redesign_physical}).
passages.judgment: The design factors identified on the pinned knee reduced torque-prediction error on the biomimetic knee. The redesigned physical routes met or exceeded the two human-muscle targets at the measured angles.

passages.question: Does the opening give researchers a reason for developing the tools and assign ownership correctly?
passages.before: This chapter presents the tools I developed to test neural controllers on a human musculoskeletal model and on models of our bipedal robot. With the software we initially used, slow simulations and manual tuning made a systematic search for controller settings impractical. The human model provided a reference for movement, but testing the robot required a model that represented where its artificial muscles pulled on the joints and how the resulting motion fed back to the controller. I built tools to construct circuits graphically, connect controllers to these mechanical models, and automate tuning. Researchers can now change a sensory connection or move an artificial muscle attachment in simulation, repeat the trial under the same conditions, and trace the effect on muscle force and leg motion.
passages.after: This chapter presents the tools I developed to test neural controllers on a human musculoskeletal model and on models of our bipedal robot. With the software we initially used, slow simulations and manual tuning made a systematic search for controller settings impractical. The human model provided a reference for movement, but testing the robot required a model that represented where its artificial muscles pulled on the joints and how the resulting motion fed back to the controller. I built tools to construct circuits graphically, connect controllers to these mechanical models, and automate tuning. Researchers can now change a sensory connection or move an artificial muscle attachment in simulation, repeat the trial under the same conditions, and trace the effect on muscle force and leg motion.
passages.judgment: The setup used for the first model made searches impractical. The opening then identifies what the tools make possible; the collaborators and earlier experiment belong in the next section.

author_confirmed_sentence.wording: With the software we initially used, slow simulations and manual tuning made a systematic search for controller settings impractical.

passages.question: Which earlier findings inform the model, and which future animal experiment can it replace?
passages.before: The honest accounting is murkier than the Three Rs framing alone suggests, because the models a robot implements are themselves products of animal experimentation. The half-center organization, the two-level rhythm and pattern architecture, and the length, force, and load signaling of the afferents were each established in preparations like the ones described above \citep{brown_intrinsic_1911, severin_1967, rybak_modelling_2006}, and the databases of afferent properties that parameterize sensory feedback are compiled from animal recordings \citep{bolen_sensory_2023}. A synthetic nervous system therefore replaces future experiments; it does not replace, and cannot repay, the animal work on which its architecture is built. Recognizing this inheritance sharpens rather than undermines the case for robotic subjects: the knowledge purchased at that cost is precisely what makes a robotic replacement scientifically meaningful, and the robot is the instrument that keeps that knowledge productive without adding to the ledger.
passages.after: Some of what we know about the spinal control of walking came from vivisection. Experiments in cats revealed that spinal circuits can generate rhythmic activity and showed how muscle receptors respond as the legs move \citep{brown_intrinsic_1911, severin_1967}. This evidence informs models of rhythm generation, muscle activation, and sensory feedback \citep{rybak_modelling_2006}. SADb brings studies of this kind together with research on human movement, computational models, and reviews \citep{bolen_sensory_2023}. With a validated model, a researcher can disable a sensory pathway and repeat the same locomotor experiment without operating on another animal. A synthetic nervous system therefore replaces future experiments.
passages.judgment: The author selected the final sentence and reserves this section’s ethical position for his own editorial judgment.

author_confirmed_sentence.wording: A synthetic nervous system therefore replaces future experiments.
author_confirmed_sentence.comment: That's the vibe I want to put out.

earlier_local_review.judgment: The paragraph identifies the historical cat experiments, other kinds of work in SADb, and a sensory intervention a researcher can repeat in a validated model.

author_instructions: Retain the stronger clause “without repeating these invasive preparations in living animals.”
Retain the complete sentence “A synthetic nervous system therefore replaces future experiments.”
Apply the same ethical standard to experiments on humans and other animals.

passages.question: Which program ran which search, and how does it select the next settings?
passages.before: For rhythm and sensory timing, the search scripts use tree-structured Parzen estimation to propose new parameter sets from earlier scores. For two Gait2392 controllers, a separate bounded least-squares fit adjusts the connections from pattern-formation channels to motor neurons to match the reference muscle recruitment. Each leg has four such channels in the reference controller (s3k) and six in the synergy-based controller (syn6). Corresponding weights are tied across sides when the fit calls for symmetry. The simulation script then loads the saved settings, records the components of its score and the reason the trial ended, and repeats a selected trial in a fresh process before an intervention.
passages.after: The Gait2392 stepping search uses Optuna \citep{akiba_optuna_2019}, and the staged rhythm and sensory-timing searches use Rustuna, its Rust implementation \citep{optuna_rustuna_2026}. Both use a tree-structured Parzen estimator, which favors settings typical of the best-scoring trials and uncommon in the rest \citep{bergstra_algorithms_2011}. For two Gait2392 controllers, a separate bounded least-squares fit adjusts the connections from pattern-formation channels to motor neurons to match the reference muscle recruitment. Each leg has four such channels in the reference controller (s3k) and six in the synergy-based controller (syn6). Corresponding weights are tied across sides when the fit calls for symmetry. The simulation script then loads the saved settings, records the components of its score and the reason the trial ended, and repeats a selected trial in a fresh process before an intervention.
passages.judgment: The Gait2392 stepping search uses Optuna. The staged rhythm and sensory-timing searches use Rustuna. The clause about the best-scoring trials explains how each program chooses settings.

passages.question: What is the design target, and what makes a run a baseline?
passages.before: I addressed these questions at four points in the design process. The actuator tests show how much tension a BPA of a given resting length can produce at a specified pressure and contraction. At the knee, that tension acts through a moment arm. The isometric tests showed how deflection under load changes the torque available from a proposed route. For controller design, I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) so a researcher can find the experiment behind a proposed feedback connection. The neuromechanical tools then let the researcher change that connection in a model and measure its effect on movement. Figure~\ref{fig:design_workflow} traces actuator sizing and route selection. Figure~\ref{fig:discussion_neuromechanical_workflow} shows how to test a change in a sensory pathway or an actuator route against the same baseline.
passages.after: I addressed these questions at four points in the design process. The actuator tests show how much tension a BPA of a given resting length can produce at a specified pressure and contraction. At the knee, that tension acts through a moment arm. The isometric tests showed how deflection under load changes the torque available from a proposed route. For controller design, I developed the Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) so that a researcher can find the experiment behind a proposed feedback connection. The neuromechanical tools then let the researcher change that connection in a model and measure its effect on movement. Figure~\ref{fig:design_workflow} shows the mechanical design process for a BPA-actuated joint, from a human torque target to the choice of actuator size and route. Figure~\ref{fig:discussion_neuromechanical_workflow} shows the neuromechanical modeling workflow. A trial with the original controller and actuator route provides the baseline. Each repeat changes one sensory pathway or one actuator route while keeping the initial pose, stimulus, and support the same.
passages.judgment: Human torque sets the joint design target. A run with the original route and controller defines the simulation baseline. The initial pose, stimulus, and support stay fixed when one component changes.
